narrative:
The model predicted a 97% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process heavily weighs this risk, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile of your class—far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students—signaled persistent academic struggle. Your LSAT score of 23.5 was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure; it sits well below the 37-point average of students who were admitted. Finally, your first-year class rank in the lowest decile (versus an average around the sixth decile for accepted applicants) added further weight in the same negative direction.

Taken together, these academic performance signals created a very high probability of bar exam failure in the model’s eyes. Gender and race played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances in the future, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Consider part-time study options that allow more preparation time, and seek targeted tutoring or bar-prep programs that address the specific gaps these records highlight. With measurable improvement in these areas, a future application could look very different. (248 words)
